messages.subject_clean: summary.hyperpar providing erroneous results
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

A few months ago I run INLA, and used pc.priors for the parameters Soak.time (random walk smoother) as seen in the file attached "rw prior". The summary.hyperpar output from this model is shown in the file attached "summary.hyperpar_FIRST"

I have not touched this model in a while, and in the meantime, I have updated INLA in my computer and also my R version.

Recently, I run this model again, using the same pc.prior formulation,  as well as the same dataset as the first time (Just wanted to check everything is fine after the updates as I am presenting this work soon)....However, as you can see in the file attached "summary.hyperpar_SECOND", the outputs are very different, particularly in the Soak_Time, fvesselID and the range of w....

What could be causing the issue? Could it be related to the definiton of the priors? Has there been any major change in the past months? Or Am I missing something else?

Also, when running this model now, I am getting the in the INLA verbose the following:

        *** WARNING *** Eigenvalue 2 of the Hessian is -14.9846 < 0
*** WARNING *** This have consequence for the accurancy of the hyperpar
*** WARNING *** Continue with a diagonal Hessian.

which I do not recall seeing before

Kind regards

Guillermo

messages.subject: INLA vs (g)lm
messages.subject_clean: INLA vs (g)lm
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm finding a few issues when I compare INLA with lm() and glm(). Could I have feedback on the issues listed below?

Thanks a lot,

Thierry

library(INLA)
ds <- data.frame(
  y = c(36831.6112941944, 35948.9994876759, 35919.1918049138, 36030.3590884849,
    35672.7335285873, 35219.7770663821, 34125.928752802),
  x = 1:7
)
inla(y ~ x, family = "gaussian", data = ds) # inla crashes
# scaling y makes inla work and the results match lm output
ds$y_scaled <- ds$y / 1000
summary(inla(y_scaled ~ x, family = "gaussian", data = ds))
summary(lm(y_scaled ~ x, data = ds))

# glm standard errors are five times smaller
# point estimates match
summary(inla(y ~ x, family = "gamma", data = ds))
summary(glm(y ~ x, family = Gamma(link = "log"), data = ds))

# the discrepancies remain after scaling
summary(inla(y_scaled ~ x, family = "gamma", data = ds))
summary(glm(y_scaled ~ x, family = Gamma(link = "log"), data = ds))

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] INLA vs (g)lm
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the scaling of the linear problem is 1) incompatible with the specified priors (the default fixed effect prior precision is 0.001, i.e. std.dev <http://std.dev>. 30, and the lm()-estimated -350 is more than 10 times larger) and 2) causes numerical issues.
1) is a model misspecification problem, which can be fixed by changing the fixed effect precision and likely also the prior for the observation precision, but that still leaves 2) causing issues, and
2) is best solved by the rescaling (what also brings the model within reasonable range of the default priors)

For the Gamma case, I'm inclined to guess it's mostly a difference between frequentist standard error and Bayesian posterior standard deviation. For large n I'd expect them to be more similar, but this sample is quite small.

Finn

Finn

messages.body_plain:
to follow up this:

for #2, its a glm() issue, see attached comparison with INLA and JAGS

in this case data are few and glm() does not produce decent uncertainty
results. this is not 'an error' with glm() but a 'feature', as it only
guaranteed to produce good results in the asymptotic limit. The only
issue is that the definition is circular:  one is within the 'asymptotic
limit' when the ``results are good''.

about #1, yes there is an issue about scaling, and INLA assumes a
'reasonable input'.

although it would be possible to internally scale everything, this only
will work for straight forward models. joint models, etc, will be hard
to scale automatically.

Best
H

messages.body_plain:
Dear Håvard and Finn,

I ran a little simulation study comparing glm and inla for the gam family. For large sample sizes, both methods yield comparable results. For smaller samples, INLA provides more robust estimates for the Gamma precision.

Best regards,

Thierry

library(INLA)
run_simulation <- function(
  n_data = 1e2, trend = -0.1, start_value = 35000, precision = 700, n_sim = 1e3
) {
  replicate(n_sim, {
    ds <- data.frame(
      x = seq(0, 10, length = n_data)
    )
    ds$mu <- log(start_value) + log(1 + trend) * ds$x
    ds$b <- precision * ds$mu
    ds$a  <- ds$mu * ds$b
    ds$y <- exp(rgamma(n_data, shape = ds$a, rate = ds$b))
    frequentist <- glm(y ~ x, family = Gamma(link = "log"), data = ds)
    bayesian <- inla(y ~ x, family = "gamma", data = ds)
    cf <- coefficients(summary(frequentist))[, c("Estimate", "Std. Error")]
    cf <- data.frame(cf)
    colnames(cf) <- c("mean", "sd")
    c(
      unlist(bayesian$summary.fixed[, c("mean", "sd")] / cf),
      freq_prec = 1 / (summary(frequentist)$dispersion * precision),
      bayes_prec = bayesian$summary.hyperpar$mean / precision
    )
  })
}

messages.subject_clean: Spatiotemporal barrier model fails to run
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to run a spatiotemporal barrier model to predict salinity in a bay area.  I successfully ran it on a spatial example without issue.  I don't think it is a memory issue because I have 64GB of RAM on a Windows virtual machine.  My data includes monthly observations of salinity for 1 year (so 12 time periods).  I've also attached a text file with the error message and verbose = T output.

Here is the relevant portions of my code:
pr = min(c(diff(range(mesh$loc[, 1])), diff(range(mesh$loc[, 2])))) /5
prior.range = c(pr, 0.9)
prior.sigma = c(1.5, 0.1)
prior.prec <- list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1.5, 0.1)))

barrier.model = inla.barrier.pcmatern(mesh, barrier.triangles = barrier.triangles, prior.range = prior.range, prior.sigma = prior.sigma)

indexs <-inla.spde.make.index("s", n.spde =barrier.model$f$n, n.group = 12)
A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc =cbind(d$x, d$y), group = d$time, n.group = 12);dim(A)

stk.e <-inla.stack(
  tag = "est",
  data = list(y=d$logv),
  A = list(1, A),
  effects = list(data.frame(m = rep(1, nrow(d))), s = indexs)
)

rprior <- list(theta = list(prior = "pccor1", param = c(0, 0.9)))
formula <- y ~ -1 + m + f(s, model = barrier.model, group = s.group, control.group = list(model = "ar1", hyper = rprior))

start.time <- Sys.time()
ressubset <- inla(formula,
            data = inla.stack.data(stk.e),
            control.predictor = list(
              compute = TRUE, link = 1,
              A = inla.stack.A(stk.e)),
            family="gaussian",
            control.family = list(hyper = prior.prec),
            control.inla= list(strategy="adaptive",int.strategy = "eb"),
            control.compute=list(cpo=TRUE),
            num.threads = "4",
            verbose = TRUE
            )

end.time <- Sys.time()
time.taken <- end.time - start.time
time.taken

Thanks,

Michael

messages.body_plain:
A quick question for the group because I'm struggling to find a definitive answer: Can R-inla (or INLA methodology in general) be used to fit ad hoc nonlinear or generalized nonlinear fixed-effect or mixed-effect regression models? If it's possible, could you point me to a good place to start learning how to do this?

Many thanks and best wishes to all,
Richard.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Richard,

it's not entirely clear what you're asking. Do you mean "nonlinear effects of covariates", as in generalised additive models? Then yes, this is what inla does best.
Can you explain/define mathematically what you mean by "random and residual effects on the nonlinear parameters"?

If you mean more fundamental types of nonlinearity with respect to the latent gaussian variables, then inlabru might help. It depends on precisely what mathematical structure you need in your model.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Nonlinear regression
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: Nonlinear regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

Many thanks for responding, I'll try and clarify the question and why I'm asking (I'm not always very precise with terminology due to not being a trained statistician, so apologies for that). I'm developing a software and interested to know if I can incorporate R-inla, but not really sure where to start.

I'm expecting the relationship between a predictor and response to follow a parametric nonlinear curve, such as a logistic curve or a normal or lognormal distribution, as in the type of model that might be fit with nlme or nlmer. e.g. for a logistic curve the objective would be to estimate the parameters 'm' (location) and 's' (scale) with respect to the predictor 'x'. I may then want to include predictors (not necessarily as fixed effects) of variation in either or both of m and s. So the first question is whether the parameters of a parametric nonlinear function of y with respect to x could be estimated in a fixed effects model?

I'm also interested in whether parametric nonlinear functions can be fitted elsewhere in the model? For example, could I use a parametric nonlinear function for change in y with respect to x to predict the autocorrelation among data points and fit this as a residual model, estimating the nonlinear parameters as part of the model fit? I'm thinking of a 1D model as a starting point, but I'm interested in more complex spatial models too.

Best wishes,
Richard.

messages.body_plain:
Hi

can you verify running

demo(Leuk)

just interrupt when the plotting start, and then look at

result$logfile

you should see around line 600, something like

[597] "Compute corrected stdev for theta[3]: negative 1.034 positive 1.005"
[598] "maxld= -2527.581 fn=177 theta= 10.867 9.335 2.140 7.361 [10.5, 0.01]"
[599] "config 0/25=[ 0.000 0.000 0.000 0.000 ] log(rel.dens)= -0.003, [0] accept, compute, 0.02s"
[600] "config 1/25=[ 0.000 -0.000 0.000 2.210 ] log(rel.dens)= -2.449, [1] accept, compute, 0.02s"
[601] "config 2/25=[ 1.117 -1.270 1.156 -1.138 ] log(rel.dens)= -2.222, [3] accept, compute, 0.02s"
[602] "config 3/25=[ -0.516 0.909 -1.053 -1.138 ] log(rel.dens)= -2.015, [2] accept, compute, 0.02s"
[603] "config 4/25=[ 2.234 0.000 0.000 -0.000 ] log(rel.dens)= -2.477, [0] accept, compute, 0.02s"

the '[3]' is the thread number, so this runs with 4 threads.

If this does not happen, try to define number of threads manually,

inla.setOption(num.threads="4:1")

and rerun demo(Leuk)

the other explanation is the 'rgeneric', as linking with libR only allow one R-interpreter, so the R-part needs to be run in serial, so
this, with smaller models take to much time that it does not look that its running in parallel, as that part will dominate. But that does not go well with serial for larger models.

btw, I just got my iMac M1 yesterday, and we will be able to provide native builds on the M1 for future versions.

Best
H

messages.subject: Predicting new observations that correspond to the posterior mean value of fixed and hyperparameters
messages.subject_clean: Predicting new observations that correspond to the posterior mean value of fixed and hyperparameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The context of below question is the aim of choosing sample size for design-based survey sampling and estimation, while having pilot data that allowed me to fit a model, useful to simulate new data.

I fitted a linear gaussian model with a categorical fixed effect and multiple random effects (specified as 'iid'). Hence, given the uncertainty (posterior distributions) of the parameters, and considering that the model can be applied to new data, this model could be thought of as representing endless possible realizations of a finite population of size N - a population defined by a single new design matrix.

I'd like to simulate random draws from just one realized population in order to choose appropriate sample size for design-based survey sampling and estimation (i.e. where uncertainty is introduced by the sampling design, while the population is regarded as fixed: the 'real' values of all discrete population units).

To represent a single population realization, the primary interest is not in the posterior distribution of the fixed and hyperparameters, but in applying one value for each parameter - an obvious choice would be the posterior mean - and having variation generated only through the (multivariate) distribution of random effects and residuals as implied by the posterior mean hyperparameter values. So values need to be drawn from this multivariate distribution, for application to new levels of the random effects and for generating new residuals.

For that purpose I use a design matrix defining observations with new levels of random effects and an appropriate configuration of fixed effect levels.

Question: I'm wondering whether I can apply an INLA function to achieve the goal of simulating these observations, especially generating the draw from the multivariate (gaussian) distribution implied by the posterior mean hyperparameter values. I could try to do it by hand, but ideally it would be possible to feed the design matrix and pass a constraint to not sample from the posterior distributions but use the mean model parameter values instead.

I have looked into lincomb and inla.posterior.sample(), but I didn't find how to use them for the above purpose.

Note: later, I may look at the posterior parameter distributions to investigate the extra effect of parameter uncertainty (especially the hyperparameters) on the precision of design-based estimates, so that is a separate step.

PS. I'm a beginning user in INLA and bayesian models.

messages.subject: Areal downscaling (disaggregation)
messages.subject_clean: Areal downscaling (disaggregation)
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA users/team,

I was wondering whether it's possible to use the R-INLA package for disaggregating areal data, namely counts.

For the sake of discussion, let $\mathcal{D}$ be the study area with spatial support consisting of $M$ non-overlapping regions, $\left\{ \mathcal{R}_{m} \right\}_{m=1}^{M}$, where $y_{m}$ denotes the observed count of $\mathcal{R}_{m}$.

The ultimate goal is to estimate the \textit{latent} counts, say $\widetilde{Y}_{n}$, corresponding to $N$ non-overlapping regions comprising a finer and misaligned spatial support, $\left\{ \mathcal{S}_{n} \right\}_{n=1}^{N}$.

Within a hierarchical framework, if $\widetilde{Y}_{n}$ is assumed to have a Poisson distribution with intensity rate $\lambda_{n}$:
$$\widetilde{Y}_{n}\mid \lambda_{n} \sim Poisson (A_{n}\lambda_{n}),$$
where $A_{n}$ is the area of $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ and $\log(\lambda_{n})=Z_{n1}\beta_{1}+\ldots+Z_{nP}\beta_{P}+U_{n}$
with $Z_{np}$ the measurement of covariate $Z_{p}$ and $U_{n}$ the spatial effect associated to $\mathcal{S}_{n}$. In this case,
$${Y}_{m} \sim Poisson(\sum_{n:\mathcal{S}_{n}\cap\mathcal{R}_{m}\neq\emptyset}A_{mn}\lambda_{n}),$$
where $A_{mn}$ is the area of $\mathcal{S}_{n}\cap\mathcal{R}_{m}$.

Further, the prior for the set of spatial effects $\mathbf{U}$ is an IGMRF with `precision matrix' $\kappa\mathbf{W}$, where $\mathbf{W}$ is the adjacency matrix of regions $\mathcal{S}_{n}$. A fully Bayesian hierarchical model is set by specifying a multivariate normal prior for the fixed effects $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ and a Gamma hyperprior for the precision parameter $\kappa$.

Is there a way to fit this model via the inla function?

Best wishes,
Roman.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Areal downscaling (disaggregation)
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Areal downscaling (disaggregation)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Roman,

since the observation model takes the form Po(\sum_j \exp(\eta_{ij})) instead of Po(\eta_i), INLA can't do this model directly (although some have approximated it as Po(\exp(\sum_j \eta_{ij})), which isn't the same thing). We are however working on related model structures that can be implemented using the additional linearisation step in the inlabru package, which will allow this type of model. It requires some updates to the inlabru interface to allow dissimilar size of inputs and observations, that I plan to work on after my current student coursework marking period is finished.

Finn

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the current implementation of the R-INLA package has certain restrictions on the structure of the link between latent variables and observations; essentially, it supports generalised additive model structures, and the
log(lambda_i) = log(sum_j(log(eta_{ji}))
doesn't follow that restriction.
The INLA method itself doesn't necessarily require that restriction though; one can write down the theory for such models using the same derivative calculations, but it's more difficult to implement more general model families.
Inlabru gets around that by linearising the predictor and iteratively calling INLA. This yields the correct posterior mode for the estimates, but approximates some of the posterior dependency structure further than a full INLA implementation would do.

As to one-to-one vs one-to-many, that is not an issue. One observation depending on multiple latent variables is the by far modest common case, which includes simple "fixed effects" and spatial models, and _any_ additive model structure
The key is that for standard additive models, the latent variables are _added_, and the only non-linearity is the link function in the final step to conditionally independent observations.
Your model has an additional final step that breaks that structure, so the R-INLA implementation doesn't know how to deal with it (but inlabru does, though the interface needs some improvements before it's practical).

Finn

messages.subject: SVC models - dueling BYM's?
messages.subject_clean: SVC models - dueling BYM's?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm fitting a Spatially Varying Coefficient (SVC) model, where intercepts and "slopes" (effect of exposure) vary via a region-level spatially smoothed distribution. It seems that the conventional wisdom is to use a BYM model on the intercepts, but the Besag (without the extra iid terms) on the slopes.

Why is this? Why not use BYM for both? I suspect it has to do with some aliasing/confounding issues. Could someone shed some light on this issue?

Thanks in advanced!

John

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] SVC models - dueling BYM's?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] SVC models - dueling BYM's?
messages.body_plain:
I see your point. You are free to do what you want, but adding an iid
term in the SVC model, seems a little unmotivated. Think about what
happen if you have more of those, then they all esssentially just add up
to one common iid noise term, which you have already in the 'bym' model
without covariates. so it seems like you have already this term covered
by the bym term without the covariate.

so in short, I would use

f(idx, x, model='besag', constr=FALSE, scale.model=TRUE)

for each of the covariates. I would set the prior to be strict, as you
basically just want a 'correction' for the constant, like

	hyper=list(prec=list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(0.1,0.01))

and then you can add structure on top of this.

Best
H

intact.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the example code! I have looked into it and tried it. From it, I understand it is possible to force the posterior sample of parameters to be (almost) equal to their posterior mean. I was not aware of that, thanks.

To generate actual observations with the approach, probably the example with 'new data' then needs to be followed, which is in the help of inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun=). In the example, random 'noise' is inserted manually within the function applied:

fun = function(zz = NA) {
     ## theta[1] is the precision
     return (Intercept + z * zz +
             rnorm(length(zz), sd = sqrt(1/theta[1])))
 }

In that sense, the code setup for my purpose may boil down to more or less the same effort as starting from model$summary.fixed[,"mean"] and model$summary.hyperpar[,"mean"], and for each observation drawing a value for the random components and summing all terms.

Perhaps an interesting further INLA functionality could be to predict observations for a (new) design matrix in a more automated way, i.e. where an INLA function would (implicitly) apply the needed formula to the design matrix and do random noise sampling (as in the function above), based on the model object. I don't know how sensible that sounds. I think that would match what some packages offer in the frequentist world, with predict().

With regards,
Floris

> group wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > The context of below question is the aim of choosing sample size for
> > design-based survey sampling and estimation, while having pilot data
> > that allowed me to fit a model, useful to simulate new data.
> >
> > I fitted a linear gaussian model with a categorical fixed effect and
> > multiple random effects (specified as 'iid'). Hence, given the
> > uncertainty (posterior distributions) of the parameters, and
> > considering that the model can be applied to new data, this model
> > could be thought of as representing endless possible realizations of a
> > finite population of size N - a population defined by a single new
> > design matrix.
> >
> > I'd like to simulate random draws from just one realized population in
> > order to choose appropriate sample size for design-based survey
> > sampling and estimation (i.e. where uncertainty is introduced by the
> > sampling design, while the population is regarded as fixed: the 'real'
> > values of all discrete population units).
> >
> > To represent a single population realization, the primary interest is
> > not in the posterior distribution of the fixed and hyperparameters,

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Predicting new observations that correspond to the posterior mean value of fixed and hyperparameters
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Predicting new observations that correspond to the posterior mean value of fixed and hyperparameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the inlabru package version of predict() & generate() (that calls inla.posterior.sample(), and does a similar job as inla.posterior.sample.eval()) implements this automatically for model="iid" model components, so that a component called "name" with model="iid" will generate new rnorm() values via name_eval(indices), for indices that are outside of the range of the INLA::f() model definition for the component;

library(inlabru)
library(tidyverse)
data <- data.frame(name_idx = 1:100) %>%
  mutate(name_val = rnorm(100),
         mu = 100 * exp(name_val),
         y = rpois(100, mu))
comp <- ~ Intercept(1) + name(name_idx, model = "iid", mapper = bru_mapper_index(100))
fit <- bru(comp, formula = y ~ Intercept + name, family = "poisson", data = data)
newdata <- data.frame(name_idx = 1:200)
gen <- generate(fit,
                data = newdata,
                formula = ~ exp(Intercept + name_eval(name_idx)),
                n.samples = 1)
ggplot(data, aes(name_idx, mu)) +
  geom_point(aes(col = "Observed")) +
  geom_point(aes(col = "Generated"), data = cbind(newdata, mu = gen[,1])) +
  scale_y_log10()

For more general new realisations of model components, it would be possible to do this for a wider range of model components if there was an INLA function for delivering the precision matrix for each internal "config", but the combinations of main models, group models, and replicate, complicates things, since not all of those combinations have an obvious extension to new indices/values. For non-iid models, the "replicate" part would be easy to implement for new indices, but "group" would be tricky, because there isn't a unique universal extension of each model; the correct extension, if any, would be context-dependent.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] SVC models - dueling BYM's?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] SVC models - dueling BYM's?
messages.body_plain:
Håvard,

Thank you very much for this.

Regarding "strict" priors: I am interested in examining spatially-varying effects of exposure. One issue is that of spatial confounding which some address by using restricted spatial regression. However, as you know, this requires the spatial field to be orthogonal to the covariate space and may not be desired.

Judging from some of your recent papers, it appears that you recommend informative priors to deal with spatial confounding instead of restricted spatial regression. Is this the case? In my situation, spatial smoothing on the intercepts is less important, and an iid model could be used here. However, it is desirable for the slopes (effects) to be smoothed spatially. Note that the priors you suggested seem reasonable for the scaled (standardized) covariate values I'm using.

Thanks,

John

messages.subject: brms to INLA bridge
messages.subject_clean: brms to INLA bridge
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I am thinking of setting up a student project to develop a prototype frontend for R-INLA/inlabru that would match very closely with brms/rstanarm syntax so that it would be easier for people like me to switch between full MCMC and INLA in the middle of a project. Currently the barrier is IMHO quite high and I often rather wait a day for a brms fit then use INLA as that would require me to rewrite a big part of the supporting code, translate priors from sd to precision etc.

Generally some mixed workflows could IMHO be very useful e.g.

- Use INLA to quickly iterate over a set of candidate models and see which make sense and then use MCMC to get high-fidelity posterior for the final model.
- Verify that the INLA approximation is faithful to MCMC when fitting a subset of a large dataset and then make inference over the whole dataset with INLA

So my question is: has anyone tried something like this before? Do you see some reasons why this would be a bad idea? What would you see as biggest risk of such a tool?

Thanks for any feedback
Martin Modrák

the 'confounding' issue is always there, and here is a recent discussion
of it

@Article{art644,
  author =       {S. H. S{\o}rbye and J. B. Illian and D. P. Simpson and
D. Burslem and H. Rue},
  title =        {Careful prior specification avoids incautious
                  inference for log-{G}aussian {C}ox point processes},
  journal =      JRSSC,
  year =         2019,
  volume =       {68},
  number =       {3},
  pages =        {543--564},
  doi =          {10.1111/rssc.12321},

I'm aware of making the spatial component be orthogonal to the
covariates, which is simply to add those, X, say, to the extraconstr

	f(..., extraconstr=list(A=X, e=...)))

and we do not need to invent any new 'algorithms' that some seems to
suggests.

I am less convinced that this approach is the way to go in general, and
tend more to think that its a feature of the model formulation that we
have to deal/live with. it does not mean that for simple covariates,
lat/long, f.ex, this could be useful.

Best
H

messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin,
we’ve definitely been talking about this for a while. For the most part Stan can’t fit INLA’s more interesting models because it doesn’t have the appropriate sparse linear algebra.

There is also a challenge with INLA that the matrices are constructed internally in the C code and not in R. Finn and I have been talking about an R-based translation of the models for a while now (some of them are possible but not the whole thing). There are a pile of uses for it, including simulating from models (which is not easy in INLA).

If you’re interested in this (and in the linear algebra problem which is not wildly hard to solve but will take a decent bit of effort) we should have a meeting. As long as we don’t involve anyone in North America it shouldn’t be too hard to find a time (I’m in Australia). Aki is interested in this too!

Dan

On Wed, Apr 28, 2021 at 15:30 modr...@email.cz <modr...@email.cz> wrote:

> Hi,
> I am thinking of setting up a student project to develop a prototype frontend for R-INLA/inlabru that would match very closely with brms/rstanarm syntax so that it would be easier for people like me to switch between full MCMC and INLA in the middle of a project. Currently the barrier is IMHO quite high and I often rather wait a day for a brms fit then use INLA as that would require me to rewrite a big part of the supporting code, translate priors from sd to precision etc.
>
> Generally some mixed workflows could IMHO be very useful e.g.
>
> - Use INLA to quickly iterate over a set of candidate models and see which make sense and then use MCMC to get high-fidelity posterior for the final model.
> - Verify that the INLA approximation is faithful to MCMC when fitting a subset of a large dataset and then make inference over the whole dataset with INLA
>
> So my question is: has anyone tried something like this before? Do you see some reasons why this would be a bad idea? What would you see as biggest risk of such a tool?
>
> Thanks for any feedback
> Martin Modrák

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Predicting new observations that correspond to the posterior mean value of fixed and hyperparameters
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Predicting new observations that correspond to the posterior mean value of fixed and hyperparameters
messages.body_plain:
Thank you Finn, for showing how sampling is done in inlabru. I have studied your example, sharing some findings here.

Can the model formula passed to INLA be retrieved easily? After running your example, a formula can be retrieved with references BRU.response, BRU_Intercept_main_model, BRU_name_main_model and accompanying values:

> fit$.args$formula
BRU.response ~ f(Intercept, model = BRU_Intercept_main_model,
    ngroup = 1, nrep = 1, values = BRU_Intercept_values) + f(name,
    model = BRU_name_main_model, ngroup = 1, nrep = 1, values = BRU_name_values) -
    1

In accordance with the usual behaviour of inla.posterior.sample(), parameter sampling is done from the posterior distribution, so that each sample has its own value per parameter, e.g. for the Intercept:

> set.seed(12345)
> gen <- generate(fit,
+                 data = newdata,
+                 formula = ~ Intercept,
+                 n.samples = 5)
> colMeans(gen)
[1] 4.756767 4.631710 4.701174 4.800624 4.830748
> all.equal(colMeans(gen), gen[1,])
[1] TRUE

I understand this is intended and it reflects uncertainty in the parameters. But from a design-based perspective, the population is fixed, i.e. there is just one realized population (the target population from which we select and measure one sample in a survey - or simulate many). That means, when describing that population with a model, the model parameters (including standard deviation (precision) of random terms) must be fixed in order to simulate new samples from that one population.

Applying the hack proposed by Håvard may counter this for inlabru as well:

fit2 <- bru(comp, formula = y ~ Intercept + name, family = "poisson", data = data,
           options = list(control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb")))
> fit2$.args$control.inla$int.strategy
[1] "eb"
scale.factor <- 10^6
for (i in length(fit2$misc$configs$config)) {
    fit2$misc$configs$config[[i]]$Q <- fit2$misc$configs$config[[i]]$Q * scale.factor
}
set.seed(12345)
gen2 <- generate(fit2,
                data = newdata,
                formula = ~ exp(Intercept),
                n.samples = 5)
> colMeans(gen2)
[1] 4.713945 4.713795 4.713857 4.713821 4.713891
> all.equal(colMeans(gen2), gen2[1,])
[1] TRUE

Then however, when sampling exp(Intercept + name_eval(name_idx)), the generated observations for name_idx 1:100 remain the same between samples, while those for 101:200 differ between samples:

set.seed(12345)
gen2 <- generate(fit2,

                data = newdata,
                formula = ~ exp(Intercept + name_eval(name_idx)),

                n.samples = 5)

ggplot(data, aes(name_idx, mu)) +
    geom_point(aes(col = "Observed")) +

    geom_point(aes(col = "Generated1"), data = cbind(newdata, mu = gen2[,1])) +
    geom_point(aes(col = "Generated2"), shape = 21, data = cbind(newdata, mu = gen2[,2])) +
    scale_y_log10()

Probably I lack background to understand what's going on in this case.

So currently I'm still inclined to take control in a manual way, as suggested in my previous post.

With regards
Floris

Op maandag 26 april 2021 om 13:06:43 UTC+2 schreef finn.l...@gmail.com:

> Hi,
>
> the inlabru package version of predict() & generate() (that calls inla.posterior.sample(), and does a similar job as inla.posterior.sample.eval()) implements this automatically for model="iid" model components, so that a component called "name" with model="iid" will generate new rnorm() values via name_eval(indices), for indices that are outside of the range of the INLA::f() model definition for the component;
>
> library(inlabru)
> library(tidyverse)
> data <- data.frame(name_idx = 1:100) %>%
>   mutate(name_val = rnorm(100),
>          mu = 100 * exp(name_val),
>          y = rpois(100, mu))
> comp <- ~ Intercept(1) + name(name_idx, model = "iid", mapper = bru_mapper_index(100))
> fit <- bru(comp, formula = y ~ Intercept + name, family = "poisson", data = data)
> newdata <- data.frame(name_idx = 1:200)
> gen <- generate(fit,
>                 data = newdata,
>                 formula = ~ exp(Intercept + name_eval(name_idx)),
>                 n.samples = 1)
> ggplot(data, aes(name_idx, mu)) +
>   geom_point(aes(col = "Observed")) +
>   geom_point(aes(col = "Generated"), data = cbind(newdata, mu = gen[,1])) +
>   scale_y_log10()
>
> For more general new realisations of model components, it would be possible to do this for a wider range of model components if there was an INLA function for delivering the precision matrix for each internal "config", but the combinations of main models, group models, and replicate, complicates things, since not all of those combinations have an obvious extension to new indices/values. For non-iid models, the "replicate" part would be easy to implement for new indices, but "group" would be tricky, because there isn't a unique universal extension of each model; the correct extension, if any, would be context-dependent.
>
> Finn
>
> On Mon, 26 Apr 2021 at 11:20, 'florisvdh' via R-inla discussion group <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > Thanks for the example code! I have looked into it and tried it. From it, I understand it is possible to force the posterior sample of parameters to be (almost) equal to their posterior mean. I was not aware of that, thanks.
> >
> > To generate actual observations with the approach, probably the example with 'new data' then needs to be followed, which is in the help of inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun=). In the example, random 'noise' is inserted manually within the function applied:
> >
> > fun = function(zz = NA) {
> >      ## theta[1] is the precision
> >      return (Intercept + z * zz +
> >              rnorm(length(zz), sd = sqrt(1/theta[1])))
> >  }
> >
> > In that sense, the code setup for my purpose may boil down to more or less the same effort as starting from model$summary.fixed[,"mean"] and model$summary.hyperpar[,"mean"], and for each observation drawing a value for the random components and summing all terms.
> >
> > Perhaps an interesting further INLA functionality could be to predict observations for a (new) design matrix in a more automated way, i.e. where an INLA function would (implicitly) apply the needed formula to the design matrix and do random noise sampling (as in the function above), based on the model object. I don't know how sensible that sounds. I think that would match what some packages offer in the frequentist world, with predict().
> >
> > With regards,
> > Floris
> >
> > Op zaterdag 24 april 2021 om 13:09:23 UTC+2 schreef he...@r-inla.org:
> > >
> > > sorry for late reply, but your question was a bit involved to
> > > understand.

> > > H
> > >

> > >
> > >
> > > On Wed, 2021-04-21 at 11:31 -0700, 'florisvdh' via R-inla discussion
> > > group wrote:
> > > > Hi,
> > > >
> > > > The context of below question is the aim of choosing sample size for
> > > > design-based survey sampling and estimation, while having pilot data
> > > > that allowed me to fit a model, useful to simulate new data.
> > > >
> > > > I fitted a linear gaussian model with a categorical fixed effect and
> > > > multiple random effects (specified as 'iid'). Hence, given the
> > > > uncertainty (posterior distributions) of the parameters, and
> > > > considering that the model can be applied to new data, this model
> > > > could be thought of as representing endless possible realizations of a
> > > > finite population of size N - a population defined by a single new
> > > > design matrix.
> > > >
> > > > I'd like to simulate random draws from just one realized population in
> > > > order to choose appropriate sample size for design-based survey
> > > > sampling and estimation (i.e. where uncertainty is introduced by the
> > > > sampling design, while the population is regarded as fixed: the 'real'
> > > > values of all discrete population units).
> > > >
> > > > To represent a single population realization, the primary interest is

> [1] TRUE

messages.subject: Modelling continuous covariates using RW2 latent model
messages.subject_clean: Modelling continuous covariates using RW2 latent model
messages.body_plain:
I am looking to model a couple of continuous covariates using a second order random walk (RW2) latent model that allows for possible non-linear relationships.

When I tried to use the code f(tmean, model = "rw2"), I received the error message that the locations were too close: min(diff(sort(x)))/diff(range(x)) = 3.319e-09 < 1e-03 and that I could fix this with some kind of binning and to see ?inla.group.

I found the code on how to use inla.group to reduce the number of unique values, and will try  it. However, when I was looking through the online book, "Bayesian Inference with INLA" by Virgilio Gómez-Rubio, it said that RW2 could be used to model continuous variables by using the "values" argument. "In particular, the values of the covariate can be binned so that they are associated with a particular value of the vector of random effects."

What is the values argument, and is it different than using inla.group? If it is different, how do you incorporate the values argument into code for the RW2 latent model where you are modelling a non-linear relationship?

Thanks,

Kristin

messages.body_plain:
Thank you very much for this. Regarding adding a constraint to implement Restricted Spatial Regression (RSR), I'm a little confused about dimension issues. Here's some code for a super simple iid model. (I know that RSR is not really needed here, I'm just trying to understand coding issues.)

I'm simply fitting:

y_i = alpha_(r_i) + beta*x + error_i, where r_i=r, the region to which individual i belongs.

alpha_r = alpha.0 + error_alpha_r

--------------------------------------------------

require(INLA)

rm(list=ls())
set.seed(1)

N <- 100

num.grps <- 10
grp <- sample(1:num.grps,N,rep=T)

sd.alpha <- 1
alpha.0 <- 3
alphas <- rnorm(num.grps,alpha.0,sd.alpha)

beta <- 0.2

x <- rnorm(N)
y <- alphas[grp] + beta * x + rnorm(N,sd=0.1)

dat <- data.frame(x,y)

require(INLA)
f <- y ~ 1 + f(grp,model="iid") + x
mod.inla <- inla(f,data=dat)

X <- mod.inla$model.matrix

P <- X %*% solve(t(X)%*%X) %*% t(X)
A.rsr <- diag(nrow(P)) - P
e.rsr <- rep(0,nrow(A.rsr))

f.rsr <- y ~ 1 + f(grp,
                   extraconstr=list(A=as.matrix(A.rsr),
                                    e=rep(0,nrow(A.rsr))),
                   ) + x

## Dimension Error
mod.inla.rst <- inla(f.rsr,data=dat)

more confusion...].

yes, either you have to fix those manually, or 'inla.group' is an
automated alternative.

Thanks again for this. All is fine with the iid model, but when I use a spatial model (e.g. bym or besag) using your code, I again get a dimension error, even using "values=1:N".

I suppose the dimension of the graph is an issue? Note that A has N columns while the graph will have size of num.grp.

Of course it will work if I create an A matrix derived from an X matrix with binned covariate values so the number of rows of X equals num.grp. This can be achieve by using, within each grp, median values for continuous covariates or perhaps modal values for categorical covariates. However it would seem that I would lose a lot of information this way.

John
